stem:
During a health check at her surgery, a 52-year-old woman asks the practice nurse which habits could make cancer of the gullet more likely.

Which factor increases her risk?

options.A: Eating plenty of fruit and vegetables
options.B: Drinking green tea at moderate temperature
options.E: Keeping a healthy body mass index

correct_answer: D. Cigarette smoking
why_correct: Tobacco smoking is an established risk factor for both squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus. The risk is greatest for squamous cell carcinoma, particularly when combined with heavy alcohol intake.
why_wrong: A. A diet high in fruit and vegetables is thought to be protective. B. Moderate-temperature tea is not a risk factor; only very hot drinks have been linked with squamous cancer. C. Aspirin is not a risk factor and may slightly lower some GI cancer risks. E. A healthy BMI lowers risk, whereas obesity increases adenocarcinoma risk through reflux.
pearl: Smoking and alcohol mainly drive oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, while obesity, chronic reflux and Barrett's oesophagus mainly drive adenocarcinoma.
thinking: Patient asks about oesophageal cancer risk ↓ Most options are neutral or protective ↓ Smoking damages oesophageal mucosa ↓ Linked with both histological types ↓ Smoking is the risk factor
exam_trap: B, Green tea — very hot drinks are linked with squamous cancer, which can make any tea option tempting, but drinking it at moderate temperature carries no such risk.
takeaway: Smoking increases the risk of oesophageal cancer, especially squamous cell carcinoma.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman with known cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department by her husband because she has become drowsy and muddled over two days. The doctor asks her to stretch out her arms and cock her wrists back. Her hands repeatedly drop forward and jerk back up in an irregular flapping movement.

What is this sign?
correct_answer: E. Asterixis
why_correct: Asterixis is a negative myoclonus: brief lapses in postural muscle tone cause the outstretched, dorsiflexed hands to flap downwards and recover. In a confused patient with cirrhosis it points to hepatic encephalopathy, although it is also seen in uraemia and carbon dioxide retention.
why_wrong: A. A resting tremor, as in Parkinson's disease, is rhythmic and occurs at rest rather than on holding a posture. B. Positive myoclonus is a sudden muscle contraction, whereas this sign is a loss of tone. C. An intention tremor appears on reaching for a target and suggests cerebellar disease. D. Fasciculations are fine twitches within a muscle and do not move the hand.
pearl: Hepatic encephalopathy is usually triggered by a precipitant such as infection, GI bleeding, constipation, sedatives or electrolyte disturbance, so always search for one; lactulose is first-line treatment.
thinking: Cirrhosis with new drowsiness and confusion ↓ Arms outstretched with wrists extended ↓ Irregular downward flapping ↓ Lapses in postural tone ↓ Asterixis of hepatic encephalopathy
exam_trap: B, Myoclonic jerks — asterixis is technically a form of myoclonus, but it is negative (loss of tone), and the named sign for this flap is asterixis.
takeaway: A flapping tremor of the outstretched, dorsiflexed hands in a confused patient with cirrhosis is asterixis.

stem:
A 34-year-old man receiving chemotherapy calls NHS 111 because swallowing has become very sore over three days. He says food and drink go down without sticking or getting stuck, but every mouthful hurts as it passes.

Which term best describes his main symptom?
correct_answer: B. Odynophagia
why_correct: Odynophagia is pain on swallowing. He has no difficulty getting food down, which rules out dysphagia; the problem is pain as the bolus passes. In an immunosuppressed patient it should raise suspicion of infective oesophagitis such as candida or herpes.
why_wrong: A. Globus is a feeling of a lump in the throat between swallows, not pain while swallowing. C. Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing, which he denies. D. Dyspepsia describes upper abdominal discomfort, fullness or indigestion. E. Regurgitation is effortless return of food or acid into the mouth.
pearl: In people who are immunosuppressed, odynophagia is commonly due to oesophageal candidiasis, often accompanied by oral thrush.
thinking: Swallowing is painful ↓ No sticking or obstruction ↓ Pain rather than difficulty ↓ Painful swallowing is odynophagia ↓ Consider infective oesophagitis in immunosuppression
exam_trap: C, Dysphagia — the two words are often confused, but dysphagia refers to difficulty swallowing, whereas his food passes freely and simply hurts.
takeaway: Odynophagia is painful swallowing; dysphagia is difficult swallowing.

stem:
At a GP review, a 29-year-old man describes several months of a gnawing ache in the upper abdomen that comes on after meals. He often cannot finish a normal portion because he feels full early, and he sometimes feels bloated. He has no trouble swallowing, no vomiting and his weight is steady.

Which term best describes this group of symptoms?
correct_answer: A. Dyspepsia
why_correct: Dyspepsia is an umbrella term for upper GI symptoms such as epigastric pain or discomfort, postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating and nausea. His post-meal epigastric ache with fullness fits this, and the absence of dysphagia, vomiting or weight loss means there are no alarm features.
why_wrong: B. Odynophagia is pain on swallowing, which he does not have. C. Steatorrhoea is pale, greasy, offensive stool from fat malabsorption. D. Tenesmus is a feeling of incomplete rectal emptying. E. Biliary colic is severe episodic right upper quadrant pain lasting hours, not chronic post-meal fullness.
pearl: In people with uninvestigated dyspepsia and no alarm features, NICE advises lifestyle and medication review and either H. pylori test and treat or a PPI trial.
thinking: Chronic upper abdominal discomfort after food ↓ Early fullness and bloating ↓ No dysphagia, vomiting or weight loss ↓ Upper GI symptom complex without alarm features ↓ Dyspepsia
exam_trap: E, Biliary colic — post-meal pain can suggest gallstones, but biliary colic is severe, episodic right upper quadrant pain rather than persistent fullness and bloating.
takeaway: Epigastric discomfort, early satiety and postprandial fullness are together called dyspepsia.

stem:
A ward nurse is recording a handover on a man admitted overnight with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. She wants to document his symptom with the correct term.

Which description fits haematemesis?

options.A: Coughing up frothy blood from the chest
options.B: Bringing up fresh red blood or dark coffee-ground material in vomit
options.D: Noticing bright red blood on the toilet paper after wiping
options.E: Passing dark red blood mixed with stool

correct_answer: B. Bringing up fresh red blood or dark coffee-ground material in vomit
why_correct: Haematemesis means vomiting blood. Fresh red blood suggests brisk bleeding, while coffee-ground material is blood that has been altered by gastric acid. Both point to bleeding proximal to the duodenojejunal flexure, such as from a peptic ulcer or varices.
why_wrong: A. Coughing up blood is haemoptysis, from the respiratory tract. C. Black, tarry, offensive stool is melaena. D. Blood on the paper after wiping suggests an anal source such as haemorrhoids or a fissure. E. Dark red blood mixed with stool usually reflects a colonic source.
pearl: Use the Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment of upper GI bleeding; NICE advises endoscopy immediately after resuscitation in unstable patients and within 24 hours of admission for others.
thinking: Term to be documented is haematemesis ↓ Haem- means blood, -emesis means vomiting ↓ Vomited blood may be fresh or acid-altered ↓ Indicates upper GI source ↓ Fresh blood or coffee grounds in vomit
exam_trap: C, Black, sticky, foul-smelling stool — melaena is also a sign of upper GI bleeding, which makes it tempting, but it describes stool, not vomit.
takeaway: Haematemesis is vomiting fresh blood or coffee-ground material from an upper GI source.

stem:
A 71-year-old man attends his GP with his daughter, who has noticed he now leaves most of his dinner. He explains that after a few forkfuls he feels completely full even though he was hungry beforehand, and his trousers have become loose. Swallowing is not painful or difficult.

Which symptom is he describing?
correct_answer: B. Early satiety
why_correct: Early satiety is feeling full after eating much less than usual. He still feels hungry before meals, so this is not loss of appetite, and swallowing is normal. With weight loss in an older person it is a concerning upper GI symptom that may reflect gastric cancer or outlet obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Anorexia means loss of appetite, but he is hungry before eating. C. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing, which he denies. D. Odynophagia is painful swallowing, which he denies. E. Nausea is a feeling of wanting to vomit, which he does not describe.
pearl: Upper abdominal symptoms with weight loss in an older adult are alarm features that warrant urgent assessment for upper GI cancer.
thinking: Reduced intake noticed by family ↓ Hungry before meals but full after small amounts ↓ Swallowing normal ↓ Feeling full early is early satiety ↓ With weight loss, consider upper GI malignancy
exam_trap: A, Anorexia — he is eating less and losing weight, which suggests poor appetite, but he describes hunger that is cut short by fullness, not lack of desire to eat.
takeaway: Feeling full after only a small amount of food, despite hunger, is early satiety.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman with no family history of diabetes is found to have a raised HbA1c on routine bloods. She has lost weight without trying over the last few months and has vague back discomfort. Her GP considers whether pancreatic disease could explain the findings.

Which statement best explains why?

options.A: Type 1 diabetes commonly first appears at this age with weight gain
options.B: Pancreatic cancer typically causes recurrent hypoglycaemia
options.C: Pancreatic cancer can present with new-onset diabetes and weight loss
options.D: Any new diabetes over the age of 60 confirms pancreatic cancer
options.E: Weight loss always reflects poor glycaemic control rather than other causes

correct_answer: C. Pancreatic cancer can present with new-onset diabetes and weight loss
why_correct: Pancreatic cancer can disrupt islet function and cause new-onset diabetes, sometimes before other symptoms appear. NICE recommends considering an urgent CT scan in older adults with weight loss and new-onset diabetes. Her back discomfort adds to the concern.
why_wrong: A. Type 1 diabetes is much less common than type 2 at this age and causes weight loss, not weight gain. B. Most pancreatic cancers cause hyperglycaemia; hypoglycaemia occurs only with rare insulin-secreting tumours. D. Most new diabetes in older adults is type 2, so it is a warning feature, not a diagnosis. E. Weight loss can come from hyperglycaemia, but unexplained weight loss in this context should prompt a search for malignancy.
pearl: Pancreatic cancer often presents late with vague symptoms such as back pain, weight loss, new diabetes or painless obstructive jaundice.
thinking: Older adult with new diabetes ↓ Unintentional weight loss and back discomfort ↓ Pancreatic cancer can impair islet function ↓ New diabetes is a recognised early clue ↓ Consider urgent CT
exam_trap: D, Any new diabetes over 60 confirms pancreatic cancer — it overstates the link; new-onset diabetes is a red flag only, and most cases are type 2.
takeaway: New-onset diabetes with weight loss in an older adult should prompt consideration of pancreatic cancer.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong A reworded: removed inaccurate 'late-onset type 1 is uncommon' claim; now type 1 is less common than type 2 at this age and causes weight loss

stem:
A 74-year-old woman from a care home is reviewed by the visiting GP because staff report she is eating less and her clothes no longer fit. She describes a constant ache in the upper abdomen and feels full after a few mouthfuls. Blood tests show iron-deficiency anaemia.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?
correct_answer: E. Gastric cancer
why_correct: Persistent upper abdominal pain, early satiety, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia in an older person are typical features of gastric cancer. These are alarm features, and she needs urgent assessment with endoscopy via a suspected cancer pathway.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome does not begin in old age with weight loss and anaemia. B. Gallstones cause episodic right upper quadrant pain, not progressive early satiety and anaemia. C. Functional dyspepsia is a diagnosis made only after alarm features are excluded. D. Chronic pancreatitis usually follows heavy alcohol use and causes steatorrhoea and diabetes.
pearl: Gastric cancer may be suggested on examination by a left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node) or a periumbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule).
thinking: Older patient with upper abdominal pain ↓ Early satiety and weight loss ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ Alarm features for upper GI malignancy ↓ Suspect gastric cancer and refer urgently
exam_trap: C, Functional dyspepsia — upper abdominal discomfort and fullness fit dyspepsia, but the label cannot be applied when weight loss and anaemia are present.
takeaway: Early satiety, weight loss and anaemia in an older adult suggest gastric cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 46-year-old teacher sees an advanced nurse practitioner about pain over his left cheek that worsens when he bends forward. For almost two weeks his nose has been blocked and he has been blowing out thick green mucus, mostly from the left side. His teeth are not sensitive to hot or cold and the pain is a dull pressure rather than electric shocks.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
correct_answer: B. Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
why_correct: Nasal obstruction with purulent, mainly one-sided discharge and maxillary pain worse on leaning forward, persisting beyond 10 days, fits acute rhinosinusitis with a likely bacterial component. Most cases still resolve without antibiotics, so NICE advises no antibiotic or a back-up prescription, with immediate antibiotics only for people who are systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis gives itching, sneezing and clear watery discharge, not purulent one-sided mucus with facial pain. C. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, electric shock-like pains without nasal symptoms. D. A dental abscess would usually cause tooth pain and temperature sensitivity. E. Cluster headache causes severe periorbital attacks lasting under a few hours with tearing and a runny nose, not constant pressure.
pearl: Unilateral nasal symptoms that persist or are accompanied by bleeding, eye or neurological signs need ENT assessment to exclude a tumour or complication such as orbital cellulitis.
thinking: Blocked nose for almost two weeks ↓ Thick purulent discharge mainly on one side ↓ Cheek pain worse on bending forward ↓ No dental or neuralgic features ↓ Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
exam_trap: D, Dental abscess — maxillary sinus pain can mimic upper tooth pain, but the nasal obstruction and purulent discharge without tooth sensitivity point to the sinus.
takeaway: Facial pain with nasal blockage and purulent discharge lasting over 10 days suggests acute bacterial rhinosinusitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct antibiotic advice aligned to NICE NG79 (no antibiotic or back-up prescription; immediate only if systemically very unwell or high risk of complications)

stem:
A 63-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is still receiving immunotherapy. At his oncology review he says breathlessness now stops him walking to the bathroom and is making him frightened. He wants to continue cancer treatment if possible.

Which approach best reflects good palliative care?

options.A: Pause the breathlessness discussion until the next scan shows whether the cancer has progressed
options.B: Refer to palliative care only once oncological treatment has been stopped
options.C: Avoid discussing what the future may hold to reduce his anxiety
options.D: Treat his breathlessness and anxiety now, alongside his cancer treatment and according to his priorities
options.E: Increase his immunotherapy dose to improve his breathing more quickly

correct_answer: D. Treat his breathlessness and anxiety now, alongside his cancer treatment and according to his priorities
why_correct: Palliative care is based on need, not prognosis or the end of active treatment. Distressing breathlessness should be assessed and managed now, for example by addressing reversible causes and using breathing techniques, a handheld fan and low-dose opioids if needed, while disease-directed treatment continues in line with his wishes.
why_wrong: A. Delaying symptom control leaves him suffering unnecessarily. B. Palliative care can and should run alongside active treatment. C. Honest, sensitive conversations about the future are part of good care and often reduce anxiety. E. Changing the dose of cancer treatment is not a way to control symptoms and would be unsafe.
pearl: Low-dose oral morphine can relieve breathlessness in advanced disease, and a handheld fan directed at the face is a simple, effective non-drug measure.
thinking: Advanced cancer with distressing breathlessness ↓ Still wants active treatment ↓ Palliative care is needs-based ↓ Treat symptoms now alongside disease treatment ↓ Guided by his goals
exam_trap: B, Refer only once treatment has stopped — many think palliative care means end-of-life care, but early involvement alongside active treatment improves symptoms and quality of life.
takeaway: Palliative symptom control should be offered as soon as it is needed, alongside disease-directed treatment.

stem:
A 38-year-old office worker tells her GP that for over a year she has opened her bowels only twice a week. Stools are hard and she has to strain. She drinks little during the day, rarely eats vegetables and takes no exercise. Her weight is stable and there is no rectal bleeding, change in pattern or family history of bowel cancer.

What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Prescribe loperamide to settle her bowel pattern
options.B: Refer for colonoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway
options.C: Start a stimulant laxative and continue indefinitely
options.E: Advise more fibre, regular fluids and physical activity

correct_answer: E. Advise more fibre, regular fluids and physical activity
why_correct: For chronic constipation without alarm features, the first step is lifestyle advice: gradually increasing dietary fibre, keeping well hydrated and increasing activity. Her low fibre and fluid intake and sedentary job make these measures particularly relevant. If they are not enough, a bulk-forming laxative is the usual first drug.
why_wrong: A. Loperamide slows the gut and would worsen constipation. B. There are no red flags to justify an urgent cancer referral. C. A stimulant laxative is not the first step and long-term use without review is not advised. D. A low-residue diet reduces stool bulk and would make constipation worse.
pearl: Bulk-forming laxatives such as ispaghula husk are first-line drugs for chronic constipation, and need adequate fluid intake to work.
thinking: Long-standing infrequent hard stools ↓ Low fibre, low fluid and inactivity ↓ No alarm features ↓ Lifestyle modification first ↓ Add bulk-forming laxative if needed
exam_trap: C, Stimulant laxative — it works quickly and is commonly prescribed, but lifestyle measures and then a bulk-forming agent come first for uncomplicated chronic constipation.
takeaway: Chronic constipation without red flags is managed first with more fibre, fluids and exercise.

stem:
Three weeks after his GP added bendroflumethiazide for hypertension, a 61-year-old man books a telephone appointment. He says he can no longer maintain an erection, which had never been a problem before. He has no urinary symptoms, morning erections are now absent and he is otherwise well.

What should the GP do first?

options.A: Arrange a prostate-specific antigen test under the suspected cancer pathway
options.B: Explain that this is an expected part of ageing and needs no action
options.C: Refer to urology for penile duplex ultrasound
options.D: Prescribe testosterone replacement without further assessment
options.E: Review his recently started medicines as a likely cause

correct_answer: E. Review his recently started medicines as a likely cause
why_correct: The problem began shortly after a thiazide diuretic was started, and thiazides are a well-recognised cause of erectile dysfunction. Reviewing his medicines and discussing an alternative antihypertensive is the logical first step, alongside a general assessment of cardiovascular risk. Invasive or specialist tests are not needed before a reversible drug cause has been considered.
why_wrong: A. Erectile dysfunction alone, without urinary or other worrying features, is not an indication for a suspected cancer referral. B. A sudden change linked in time to a new drug should not be dismissed as ageing. C. Specialist vascular imaging is not a first-line step when a medication cause is likely. D. Testosterone is only considered after confirmed low levels and is not a first step here.
pearl: Common drug causes of erectile dysfunction include thiazides, beta-blockers, SSRIs, antipsychotics, finasteride and opioids.
thinking: New erectile dysfunction ↓ Clear temporal link to a newly started thiazide ↓ Thiazides are a recognised cause ↓ No red flags needing urgent tests ↓ Review the medication first
exam_trap: C, Referring to urology for duplex scanning — it sounds thorough, but specialist imaging is not needed before a simple, reversible drug cause has been addressed.
takeaway: When erectile dysfunction follows a new prescription, review the medicines before anything else.

presentation: Anticipatory prescribing at the end of life
stem:
A district nurse rings the GP about Margaret, an 84-year-old woman with end-stage heart failure who has chosen to die at home. She is now bed-bound, sleeping most of the day and taking only sips of fluid. At the moment she is comfortable, but the nurse is worried about how symptoms will be managed overnight or at the weekend.

Which course of action is most appropriate?

options.A: Wait until a symptom becomes severe and then arrange an urgent prescription
options.B: Start a continuous sedative infusion now to prevent distress
options.C: Avoid talking to her family about symptoms that might develop
options.D: Prescribe individualised as-needed medicines in advance for likely symptoms
options.E: Prescribe the maximum standard doses of all syringe driver drugs immediately

correct_answer: D. Prescribe individualised as-needed medicines in advance for likely symptoms
why_correct: Margaret is in the last days of life and is likely to develop pain, breathlessness, agitation, nausea or noisy respiratory secretions. NICE NG31 advises individualised anticipatory prescribing so that suitable medicines and doses are already in the home and can be given promptly by the community team when needed. Choices should reflect her current medicines, renal function and wishes.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for severe symptoms leads to avoidable distress and delays, especially out of hours. B. Sedation is not given routinely when she is comfortable; medicines are prescribed for use only if needed. C. Discussing likely changes with the family helps them prepare and supports shared planning. E. Doses should be individualised and started low, not set at standard maximum levels.
pearl: Anticipatory medicines usually cover pain, breathlessness, agitation, nausea and vomiting, and respiratory secretions, with clear instructions on indication, dose and route.
thinking: Dying at home and currently comfortable ↓ Symptoms likely to develop in the last days ↓ Delays are likely out of hours ↓ Medicines can be prescribed in advance for use if needed ↓ Individualised anticipatory prescribing
exam_trap: B, Starting a continuous sedative infusion — it seems to prevent distress, but sedating someone who is comfortable is not justified; medicines are given only when a symptom actually arises.
takeaway: Prescribe individualised as-needed medicines in advance for people expected to die soon.

stem:
A 70-year-old man with motor neurone disease is being cared for at home and is expected to die within weeks. His daughter, who lives with him, has noticed a box of injectable medicines left by the hospice team and asks the GP on a home visit what they are for. He currently takes regular oral morphine and is comfortable.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: They will replace his oral morphine with a syringe driver from today
options.B: They are intended to slow the progression of his illness
options.C: They will keep him continuously sedated from now on
options.D: They allow symptoms that are likely to develop to be treated quickly
options.E: They mean that further discussions about his care are no longer needed

correct_answer: D. They allow symptoms that are likely to develop to be treated quickly
why_correct: Anticipatory, or just in case, medicines are prescribed ahead of time so that predictable end-of-life symptoms such as pain, breathlessness, agitation and secretions can be treated without delay by visiting clinicians. They are used only if and when symptoms occur. His current oral regimen continues while he can swallow and remains comfortable.
why_wrong: A. They do not replace his effective oral analgesia; a syringe driver is started only if he can no longer take oral medicines or needs it. B. They are for symptom relief, not to modify the disease. C. They are not for routine sedation; each is given for a specific symptom when it arises. E. Ongoing conversations with the family and care planning remain essential.
pearl: Just in case medicines are kept in the home with a signed administration authorisation so that community nurses can give them promptly, including out of hours.
thinking: Expected to die at home ↓ Currently comfortable on oral morphine ↓ Medicines left in advance ↓ Given only if predictable symptoms appear ↓ Purpose is prompt symptom relief
exam_trap: A, Switching to a syringe driver now — the injectable drugs look like a replacement, but he is comfortable and can swallow, so his oral regimen continues.
takeaway: Anticipatory medicines are there so likely end-of-life symptoms can be treated promptly if they arise.

stem:
Following a hospice referral, a 59-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer tells her GP she is frightened that palliative care means she will have to leave home and stop all her medicines. Her oncologist has advised that no further treatment will cure the cancer, and she has ongoing nausea and low mood.

Which statement best describes what palliative care aims to provide?

options.A: Further treatment intended to cure the primary tumour
options.B: Planned admission to an acute hospital ward for her remaining care
options.C: Withdrawal of all medicines to avoid side effects
options.D: Relief of symptoms and support to achieve the best possible quality of life
options.E: Automatic transfer to intensive care if she becomes unwell

correct_answer: D. Relief of symptoms and support to achieve the best possible quality of life
why_correct: Palliative care aims to relieve physical symptoms such as nausea and to address psychological, social and spiritual needs, so that people with life-limiting illness live as well as possible. It can be delivered at home, in a hospice or in hospital according to the person's wishes. Medicines are continued or started where they help symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Curative treatment is no longer available, and palliative care is not aimed at cure. B. Care can be provided wherever she prefers, including at home. C. Medicines such as antiemetics are often central to symptom control. E. Intensive care is not a routine part of palliative care and may not match her goals.
pearl: Palliative care can begin early alongside other treatment, not only in the last days of life.
thinking: Incurable cancer ↓ Fears about leaving home and stopping medicines ↓ Palliative care can be delivered at home ↓ Focus is on symptoms and wider needs ↓ Aim is quality of life
exam_trap: C, Stopping all medicines — this matches what she fears, but effective drugs for nausea, pain and mood are a key part of palliative care.
takeaway: Palliative care aims to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life, wherever the person chooses to be cared for.

presentation: Individualised symptom control in palliative care
stem:
On a hospice ward round, a 72-year-old man with prostate cancer and bone metastases reports that his back pain keeps him awake despite regular paracetamol and modified-release morphine. His wife says she would rather the dose was not increased because she worries he will become addicted, and suggests the team decide for him. He is alert and able to discuss his care.

Which principle should guide management?

options.A: Assess his pain fully and tailor treatment to his needs and wishes
options.B: Limit his opioid dose to avoid dependence
options.C: Let his wife make the treatment decisions to reduce his distress
options.D: Concentrate on his physical symptoms and leave emotional concerns for later
options.E: Keep stronger opioids for the final days of life

correct_answer: A. Assess his pain fully and tailor treatment to his needs and wishes
why_correct: Palliative care is based on careful assessment of each symptom and treatment tailored to the person's own goals. His pain should be reassessed, including the possibility of bone pain needing additional measures such as radiotherapy, and his analgesia titrated. As he has capacity, he should be involved in decisions, and his wife's concerns about addiction can be explored and addressed.
why_wrong: B. Fear of dependence should not prevent adequate pain relief in advanced cancer. C. He has capacity, so decisions are made with him, not by his family on his behalf. D. Psychological and social needs are addressed alongside physical symptoms, not postponed. E. Opioids are used whenever pain needs them, not only at the very end of life.
pearl: Metastatic bone pain often responds well to single-fraction palliative radiotherapy alongside analgesia.
thinking: Uncontrolled pain despite regular analgesia ↓ Patient has capacity ↓ Family worried about addiction ↓ Reassess pain and titrate treatment ↓ Individualised care involving the patient
exam_trap: B, Limiting the opioid dose — the wife's worry about addiction can seem reasonable, but in advanced cancer under-treating pain causes real suffering and addiction is not a reason to withhold relief.
takeaway: Palliative symptom control should be assessed and tailored to each person, who should be involved in decisions.

stem:
At an NHS health check, a 47-year-old man is told his BMI is in the obese range. He points out that a friend with the same BMI is a rugby player with very little fat, and asks whether this number alone tells the nurse how unhealthy he is.

Which reply is most appropriate?

options.A: Waist measurement gives no useful information beyond BMI
options.B: BMI on its own accurately predicts his individual health risk
options.C: His risk is judged using BMI together with other measures and clinical factors
options.D: His blood pressure only needs checking if his BMI rises above 40
options.E: His cardiovascular risk depends on BMI rather than on blood pressure or cholesterol

correct_answer: C. His risk is judged using BMI together with other measures and clinical factors
why_correct: BMI is a useful screening measure but cannot distinguish muscle from fat or show where fat is stored. NICE recommends interpreting it alongside waist-to-height ratio, which reflects central adiposity, and other factors such as blood pressure, lipids, glucose, smoking and ethnicity. A broader assessment gives a better picture of his individual risk.
why_wrong: A. Waist-to-height ratio adds information about central fat, which is linked to cardiometabolic risk. B. BMI can be misleading in muscular people and does not determine individual risk alone. D. Blood pressure should be checked as part of assessment at any BMI. E. Blood pressure and cholesterol are major independent cardiovascular risk factors.
pearl: Waist-to-height ratio is a simple measure of central adiposity that NICE recommends alongside BMI in adults with a BMI below 35.
thinking: BMI in obese range ↓ BMI cannot separate muscle from fat ↓ Central adiposity adds risk information ↓ Other clinical risk factors matter ↓ Combine BMI with other measures
exam_trap: B, BMI alone predicting risk — BMI is the headline figure in most weight assessments, but it is a population tool and misses fat distribution and other risk factors.
takeaway: Interpret BMI alongside waist-to-height ratio and other clinical risk factors rather than in isolation.

stem:
A practice nurse records a high reading in a 52-year-old woman who has just hurried in from the car park and is still wearing a thick jumper. Her previous readings have been normal, and she has a large upper arm. The nurse plans to recheck it.

Which step will most improve the accuracy of the repeat reading?

options.A: Take the reading with her arm hanging loosely by her side
options.B: Use a smaller cuff so that it fits more tightly
options.C: Record only the first reading, as later readings are falsely low
options.D: Place the cuff over her jumper sleeve for comfort
options.E: Let her sit and rest, then use a cuff sized for her arm on bare skin

correct_answer: E. Let her sit and rest, then use a cuff sized for her arm on bare skin
why_correct: Recent exertion, clothing under the cuff and a cuff that is too small all falsely raise blood pressure. NICE NG136 advises measuring with the person seated and rested, the arm bare and supported at heart level, and a cuff of the correct size. If the first reading is raised, a second is taken and the lower value recorded, with ambulatory or home monitoring used to confirm hypertension.
why_wrong: A. A dependent, unsupported arm gives falsely high readings. B. A cuff that is too small overestimates blood pressure, which matters in someone with a large arm. C. A raised first reading should be repeated rather than relied upon. D. Clothing under the cuff reduces accuracy.
pearl: A raised clinic reading should be confirmed with ambulatory or home monitoring before hypertension is diagnosed.
thinking: Unexpectedly high reading ↓ Recent exertion, thick clothing and large arm ↓ All falsely raise readings ↓ Rest, bare arm, correct cuff, arm supported ↓ Repeat with good technique
exam_trap: B, Using a smaller cuff — a snug cuff feels more precise, but an undersized cuff overestimates blood pressure.
takeaway: Rest the patient and use a correctly sized cuff on a bare, supported arm before repeating a high reading.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman sees the practice pharmacist after her third bout of cystitis this year, each confirmed and treated. She works long shifts as a bus driver, rarely stops to drink and often holds on for hours before she can use a toilet. She is not pregnant and has no fever or loin pain.

Which advice is most likely to help reduce further episodes?

options.B: Drink enough fluids and empty her bladder when she needs to rather than holding on
options.C: Start a course of antibiotics herself whenever she notices any urinary discomfort
options.D: Restrict her fluid intake to reduce how often she needs to pass urine

correct_answer: B. Drink enough fluids and empty her bladder when she needs to rather than holding on
why_correct: Low fluid intake and habitually delaying voiding are modifiable factors that may contribute to recurrent cystitis. Advising adequate hydration and emptying the bladder when the urge arises is simple, safe self-care advice for recurrent uncomplicated urinary tract infection. Further options such as antibiotic prophylaxis are considered only after behavioural measures and review.
why_wrong: A. Dairy avoidance has no role in preventing urinary infection. C. Self-starting antibiotics for any discomfort without assessment promotes resistance; standby treatment is only used when agreed with a prescriber. D. Restricting fluids concentrates urine and works against prevention. E. Exercise has no link with recurrent cystitis and need not be avoided.
pearl: For recurrent UTI, NICE advises considering behavioural and personal hygiene measures and self-care before antibiotic prophylaxis.
thinking: Recurrent uncomplicated cystitis ↓ Poor fluid intake at work ↓ Habitually delays voiding ↓ Modifiable factors identified ↓ Advise hydration and regular bladder emptying
exam_trap: D, Restricting fluids — she may think fewer toilet trips would suit her job, but concentrated urine and infrequent voiding make infection more likely.
takeaway: Good hydration and not delaying urination are first-line self-care for recurrent uncomplicated UTI.

stem:
A 63-year-old lorry driver with intermittent claudication in his right calf is seen in the vascular clinic. He smokes heavily and asks why the team keeps stressing that he should stop, as his legs are the problem rather than his lungs.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Smoking speeds up the build-up of atherosclerosis in his arteries
options.B: Smoking helps new collateral vessels form in his legs
options.D: Smoking reduces his risk of arterial thrombosis
options.E: Smoking has no effect on arteries outside the heart

correct_answer: A. Smoking speeds up the build-up of atherosclerosis in his arteries
why_correct: Smoking is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis, including peripheral arterial disease. It damages the endothelium, promotes plaque formation and increases the tendency to thrombosis. Stopping slows disease progression and reduces the risk of amputation, myocardial infarction and stroke.
why_wrong: B. Smoking causes vasoconstriction and impairs, rather than helps, collateral flow. C. Smoking does not reverse plaque; stopping helps prevent progression. D. Smoking increases platelet activation and thrombotic risk. E. Smoking affects arteries throughout the body, including those of the legs.
pearl: Smoking cessation, an antiplatelet, a statin and supervised exercise are the foundations of managing intermittent claudication.
thinking: Intermittent claudication ↓ Atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease ↓ Smoking damages endothelium and promotes plaque and thrombosis ↓ Stopping slows progression ↓ Smoking accelerates atherosclerosis
exam_trap: E, Smoking has no effect on arteries outside the heart — he links smoking with lungs and heart, but atherosclerosis is systemic and the leg arteries are strongly affected.
takeaway: Smoking accelerates atherosclerosis, so stopping is central to managing peripheral arterial disease.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman with known acute intermittent porphyria is brought to the emergency department with severe colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and dark urine. Her attacks had been quiet for several years. Ten days ago a neurologist started a new medicine for trigeminal neuralgia.

Which of the following medicines is most likely to have triggered this attack?
correct_answer: C. Carbamazepine
why_correct: Many drugs that induce hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes increase demand for haem and upregulate ALA synthase, precipitating an acute porphyric attack. Carbamazepine, a first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia, is a potent enzyme inducer and is classed as unsafe in acute porphyria. The timing of a new prescription before the attack fits.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol is considered safe in acute porphyria and is used for analgesia during attacks. B. Opioids such as morphine are considered safe and are used to control the pain of an attack. D. Amoxicillin is regarded as safe. E. Gabapentin is generally regarded as a safe anticonvulsant option in acute porphyria.
pearl: Other common precipitants of acute porphyric attacks include alcohol, fasting or low-calorie diets, infection, and hormonal changes such as the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle.
thinking: Known acute intermittent porphyria ↓ Abdominal pain, vomiting, dark urine: acute attack ↓ New medicine started shortly before ↓ Enzyme-inducing drugs precipitate attacks ↓ Carbamazepine is the likely trigger
exam_trap: E, Gabapentin — it is also an anticonvulsant used for neuropathic pain, so it seems equally suspicious, but unlike carbamazepine it does not induce hepatic enzymes and is regarded as safe.
takeaway: Always check a drug's porphyria safety before prescribing; enzyme inducers such as carbamazepine can precipitate an acute attack.

stem:
A 58-year-old man has had a raised red cell count on three full blood counts over six months, with a high haematocrit each time. He feels a little muzzy-headed but is otherwise well. His GP explains that the main danger of having too many red cells is related to how thick his blood has become.

Which complication is he at greatest risk of?

options.E: Chronic infection of the ear canal

correct_answer: D. Arterial or venous thrombosis
why_correct: An increased red cell mass raises haematocrit and whole-blood viscosity, slowing flow and promoting clot formation. This makes stroke, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis and unusual-site thromboses the major complications of erythrocytosis, particularly polycythaemia vera. Reducing the haematocrit by venesection is aimed mainly at lowering this risk.
why_wrong: A. Cataracts are not caused by a raised red cell mass. B. Ureteric stones are not a recognised complication of increased viscosity. C. Polycythaemia does not lower blood glucose. E. Otitis externa has no link with red cell mass.
pearl: In polycythaemia vera, thrombosis is the leading cause of illness and death, which is why low-dose aspirin and venesection are cornerstones of management.
thinking: Persistently high red cell count and haematocrit ↓ Erythrocytosis ↓ Higher whole-blood viscosity ↓ Sluggish flow favours clotting ↓ Thrombosis is the key risk
exam_trap: B, Ureteric stone formation — high cell turnover can raise urate and cause gout, so a urate stone seems plausible, but the defining danger of a raised red cell mass is thrombosis.
takeaway: A raised red cell mass thickens the blood and chiefly increases the risk of thrombosis.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman is referred to the haematology clinic because her platelet count has been very high on repeated tests over several months. Her ferritin and CRP are normal, she has had no recent surgery, infection or bleeding, and a JAK2 mutation has been detected. She asks what problems this might cause her.

Which complication is she at risk of?

options.B: Both blood clots and episodes of bleeding
options.C: Excess iron deposition in the liver and heart
options.D: Spontaneous release of tumour contents into the blood

correct_answer: B. Both blood clots and episodes of bleeding
why_correct: With no reactive cause and a JAK2 mutation, this is essential thrombocythaemia, a myeloproliferative neoplasm. The excess platelets are often functionally abnormal, so patients are prone to arterial and venous thrombosis, yet very high counts can also cause bleeding through acquired von Willebrand syndrome. Both risks shape treatment decisions such as aspirin and cytoreduction.
why_wrong: A. Autoimmune haemolysis is not a feature of essential thrombocythaemia. C. Iron overload occurs with repeated transfusion or haemochromatosis, not a raised platelet count. D. Tumour lysis is linked to treatment of high-turnover malignancies, not a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm. E. Thyroid failure is not a complication.
pearl: Extreme thrombocytosis increases bleeding risk because large platelet numbers adsorb and clear high-molecular-weight von Willebrand factor multimers, causing acquired von Willebrand syndrome.
thinking: Persistently very high platelets ↓ No iron deficiency, inflammation or other reactive cause ↓ JAK2 positive: essential thrombocythaemia ↓ Abnormal platelets cause clots ↓ Very high counts can also cause bleeding
exam_trap: D, Spontaneous release of tumour contents — it is a blood cancer so tumour lysis comes to mind, but essential thrombocythaemia is an indolent disorder in which clotting and bleeding are the real dangers.
takeaway: Essential thrombocythaemia causes both thrombosis and, at very high counts, bleeding.

stem:
A 49-year-old man on a medical ward is reviewed after his routine bloods return. His haemoglobin is low, his white cell count is low and his platelet count is low. The consultant asks the foundation doctor to name this blood count pattern before planning further tests.

Which term describes it?
correct_answer: B. Pancytopenia
why_correct: A reduction in all three peripheral blood lineages, red cells, white cells and platelets, is called pancytopenia. It points towards marrow failure or infiltration, ineffective haematopoiesis such as B12 deficiency, hypersplenism or peripheral destruction, and should prompt a blood film and further investigation.
why_wrong: A. Leucocytosis means a raised white cell count, whereas his is low. C. Isolated thrombocytopenia involves only platelets, but all three lines are reduced. D. Erythrocytosis is an increased red cell mass, the opposite of his low haemoglobin. E. Neutrophilia is a raised neutrophil count.
pearl: Causes of pancytopenia can be grouped as reduced production (aplastic anaemia, infiltration, drugs, B12 or folate deficiency) or increased destruction or pooling (hypersplenism, autoimmune processes).
thinking: Low haemoglobin ↓ Low white cell count ↓ Low platelets ↓ All three lines reduced ↓ Pancytopenia
exam_trap: C, Isolated thrombocytopenia — the low platelet count often draws attention first, but the word isolated excludes the falls in haemoglobin and white cells.
takeaway: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together is pancytopenia, which needs a search for marrow or systemic causes.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman tells her GP she has had frequent headaches and a ruddy, flushed complexion for several months. Repeated blood counts show her haemoglobin and haematocrit are consistently above the normal range, while her white cells and platelets are normal.

Which broad haematological diagnosis best describes her problem?
correct_answer: B. Polycythaemia
why_correct: A persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit indicates an increased red cell concentration, which is polycythaemia (erythrocytosis). The extra red cells increase blood viscosity, causing headache, and the higher red cell content gives a plethoric, flushed face. It then needs evaluation for relative, secondary and primary causes.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency produces a low, not high, haemoglobin. C. Marrow aplasia causes low counts, often across all lines. D. Her platelet count is normal. E. Her white cell count is normal.
pearl: Aquagenic pruritus, itching after a warm bath or shower, is a characteristic symptom of polycythaemia vera.
thinking: Headaches and facial plethora ↓ Haemoglobin and haematocrit persistently high ↓ Other cell lines normal ↓ Increased red cell concentration ↓ Polycythaemia
exam_trap: C, Bone marrow aplasia — it is a primary marrow disorder, as polycythaemia vera is, which makes it tempting, but aplasia lowers counts rather than raising them.
takeaway: A persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit with plethora means polycythaemia.
notes: Reviewer fix: exam_trap wrongly implied many causes of polycythaemia are primary marrow disorders; reworded to polycythaemia vera

stem:
A 67-year-old man with COPD who has smoked 40 cigarettes a day since his teens attends the respiratory clinic. His face looks plethoric and he is mildly cyanosed, with resting oxygen saturation below his target range. His full blood count shows a raised haemoglobin and haematocrit.

Which explanation best accounts for the blood count?

options.A: Relative rise from reduced plasma volume due to dehydration
options.B: Folate deficiency from a poor diet
options.C: Erythropoietin-driven red cell increase due to chronic hypoxia
options.E: Iron deficiency from slow occult blood loss

correct_answer: C. Erythropoietin-driven red cell increase due to chronic hypoxia
why_correct: Chronic hypoxaemia from lung disease and carboxyhaemoglobin from heavy smoking reduce tissue oxygen delivery, so the kidneys increase erythropoietin output and the marrow makes more red cells. This appropriate, secondary polycythaemia explains his raised haemoglobin. It is distinct from polycythaemia vera, in which erythropoietin is low.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration causes a relative polycythaemia but is not suggested here and does not explain his cyanosis and low saturation. B. Folate deficiency causes a megaloblastic anaemia, not a raised haemoglobin. D. Acute bleeding lowers haemoglobin. E. Iron deficiency causes a low haemoglobin with microcytosis.
pearl: Serum erythropoietin is usually normal or raised in secondary polycythaemia but low in polycythaemia vera, which helps distinguish them.
thinking: Heavy smoker with COPD ↓ Low oxygen saturation ↓ Raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Hypoxia stimulates renal erythropoietin ↓ Secondary polycythaemia
exam_trap: A, Relative rise from reduced plasma volume — relative polycythaemia from dehydration is a real cause, but it does not explain the cyanosis and low saturations that point to hypoxic drive.
takeaway: Chronic hypoxia from lung disease or smoking causes secondary polycythaemia via raised erythropoietin.
notes: Reviewer fix: option A 'low haemoglobin masked by dehydration' was muddled; reworded to relative polycythaemia from reduced plasma volume, why_wrong A and exam_trap aligned

stem:
A 46-year-old woman sees her GP with three months of tiredness, drenching sweats and a dragging feeling under her left ribs. A large spleen is palpable. Her full blood count shows a very high white cell count with neutrophils, myelocytes and basophils on the film. Cytogenetics later identify a BCR-ABL1 fusion.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
correct_answer: D. Chronic myeloid leukaemia
why_correct: Massive splenomegaly with a marked leucocytosis showing myeloid cells at every stage of maturation and basophilia is typical of chronic myeloid leukaemia. The BCR-ABL1 fusion, produced by the t(9;22) Philadelphia translocation, defines the disease and drives a constitutively active tyrosine kinase.
why_wrong: A. Hodgkin lymphoma presents with lymphadenopathy and Reed-Sternberg cells, not BCR-ABL1. B. Myeloma causes bone pain, anaemia, hypercalcaemia and a paraprotein. C. Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated low platelets without splenomegaly. E. Iron deficiency causes microcytic anaemia, not a high white count.
pearl: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib target the BCR-ABL1 protein and have transformed the outlook in chronic phase chronic myeloid leukaemia.
thinking: Fatigue, sweats and left upper quadrant discomfort ↓ Marked splenomegaly ↓ Very high white count with left shift and basophils ↓ BCR-ABL1 fusion ↓ Chronic myeloid leukaemia
exam_trap: A, Hodgkin lymphoma — night sweats and fatigue are B symptoms that suggest lymphoma, but the very high myeloid white count and BCR-ABL1 fusion are specific to chronic myeloid leukaemia.
takeaway: BCR-ABL1 fusion (Philadelphia chromosome) defines chronic myeloid leukaemia.

stem:
A 22-year-old man with hay fever and childhood eczema has had a wheezy cough and itchy, streaming eyes since the spring. He has not travelled abroad and takes no regular medicines. His full blood count is normal apart from a raised eosinophil count.

Which broad group of conditions is the most common cause of this finding in the UK?
correct_answer: B. Atopic and allergic disorders
why_correct: In the UK, the commonest cause of a raised eosinophil count is atopic disease such as asthma, allergic rhinitis and eczema. His wheeze, seasonal eye and nose symptoms and atopic history fit this. Worldwide, parasitic infection is the leading cause, but he has no travel history.
why_wrong: A. Bleeding does not cause eosinophilia. C. Iron deficiency affects red cells and does not raise eosinophils. D. Osteoarthritis is not associated with eosinophilia. E. Dehydration may concentrate counts slightly but does not selectively raise eosinophils.
pearl: Persistent marked eosinophilia without an allergic explanation needs consideration of parasites (especially after travel), drug reactions, vasculitis such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and haematological malignancy.
thinking: Atopic history: hay fever and eczema ↓ New wheeze and allergic eye symptoms ↓ Raised eosinophils only ↓ No travel or new drugs ↓ Allergic disease is the likely cause
exam_trap: E, Volume depletion — haemoconcentration can raise measured counts, but it affects all cells and does not produce a selective rise in eosinophils.
takeaway: In the UK, eosinophilia is most often due to allergic and atopic disease.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman attends the oncology day unit for a blood test before her third cycle of chemotherapy for bowel cancer. She feels well and is apyrexial. Her report shows a normal haemoglobin and platelet count, but the neutrophils are well below the reference range.

Which term describes this result?
correct_answer: D. Neutropenia
why_correct: A neutrophil count below the lower limit of normal is neutropenia. It is a common effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy, which suppresses rapidly dividing marrow precursors, with the lowest count usually occurring one to two weeks after a cycle. It may require dose delay and puts her at risk of serious infection.
why_wrong: A. Lymphocytosis is a raised lymphocyte count. B. Thrombocytosis is a raised platelet count, whereas her platelets are normal. C. Polycythaemia is a raised red cell mass, whereas her haemoglobin is normal. E. Neutrophilia means too many neutrophils, the opposite of this result.
pearl: Patients having chemotherapy should have 24-hour access to an acute oncology helpline and be told that fever during treatment needs same-day hospital assessment.
thinking: Receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy ↓ Pre-cycle blood test ↓ Neutrophils below range, other lines normal ↓ Reduced neutrophils ↓ Neutropenia
exam_trap: E, Neutrophilia — the similar word is easily confused, but the -philia suffix denotes an increase, whereas -penia denotes a reduction.
takeaway: A reduced neutrophil count is neutropenia, a common consequence of cytotoxic chemotherapy.

stem:
A 47-year-old man's routine health-check bloods show a high haemoglobin and haematocrit, and the result is unchanged on a repeat sample a month later. He feels well, drinks moderately and smokes occasionally. There is no splenomegaly and his other counts are normal.

What is the most appropriate first step in managing this result?

options.A: Request an urgent bone marrow biopsy
options.B: Put the result down to dehydration and repeat it next year
options.C: Look systematically for relative, secondary or primary causes
options.D: Start aspirin and venesection to bring the haematocrit down
options.E: Check ferritin, because iron deficiency is the most likely cause

correct_answer: C. Look systematically for relative, secondary or primary causes
why_correct: A persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit needs a structured assessment before any treatment: relative causes such as reduced plasma volume, secondary causes such as smoking, hypoxic lung disease, sleep apnoea, testosterone use or erythropoietin-secreting tumours, and primary causes such as polycythaemia vera, usually with JAK2 testing. Treatment depends on which group applies.
why_wrong: A. Marrow biopsy is not a first-line test and is reserved for selected cases after initial work-up. B. Confirmed persistent erythrocytosis should not be dismissed or left for a year. D. Starting treatment before establishing the cause is premature. E. Iron deficiency lowers haemoglobin and does not cause erythrocytosis, although it can mask polycythaemia vera.
pearl: Smoking raises carboxyhaemoglobin and is a common, reversible secondary cause of a mildly raised haematocrit.
thinking: Raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Confirmed on repeat ↓ Persistent erythrocytosis ↓ Think relative, secondary and primary causes ↓ Structured work-up before treatment
exam_trap: D, Start aspirin and venesection — these are the mainstays of polycythaemia vera treatment, which makes them tempting, but the cause has not yet been established.
takeaway: Confirmed erythrocytosis needs a structured search for relative, secondary and primary causes before treatment.

stem:
A 19-year-old woman with beta thalassaemia major has received red cell transfusions every few weeks since early childhood. At her annual review her serum ferritin is markedly raised and her liver enzymes are mildly deranged. Her chelation adherence has been poor.

Which process best explains these results?

options.A: Hypocalcaemia from citrate in stored blood
options.B: Iron deficiency from repeated blood sampling
options.D: Scurvy due to poor vitamin C intake

correct_answer: E. Iron overload from repeated transfusion
why_correct: Each unit of red cells delivers a large amount of iron that the body has no way to excrete. With regular transfusion and poor adherence to chelation, iron accumulates in the liver, heart and endocrine organs, raising ferritin and causing liver damage. Chelation therapy, for example with desferrioxamine or deferasirox, is used to prevent this.
why_wrong: A. Citrate-related hypocalcaemia is an acute problem of massive transfusion, not a chronic cause of raised ferritin. B. Iron deficiency would lower ferritin. C. Alloantibody-mediated neutropenia is not a recognised consequence of chronic red cell transfusion and would not raise ferritin or derange liver tests. D. Vitamin C deficiency does not raise ferritin.
pearl: Cardiac iron loading is the main cause of death in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia and is monitored with T2* cardiac MRI.
thinking: Regular transfusions for many years ↓ Poor adherence to chelation ↓ Very high ferritin ↓ Deranged liver tests from iron deposition ↓ Transfusional iron overload
exam_trap: A, Hypocalcaemia from citrate — a recognised transfusion complication, but it occurs acutely during massive transfusion and does not raise ferritin.
takeaway: Chronic transfusion without effective chelation causes iron overload affecting the liver, heart and endocrine glands.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong C described red cell alloimmunisation, not the option's alloantibody neutropenia; rewritten to match

stem:
A 16-year-old boy with sickle cell anaemia comes to the emergency department with severe pain in his back, thighs and chest that began after a viral illness and a cold, wet football match. He is dehydrated. His mother asks what is happening inside his body to cause the pain.

What is the underlying mechanism?

options.A: Destruction of platelets by antibodies in the spleen
options.B: Blockage of small blood vessels by sickled red cells
options.C: Failure to absorb vitamin K from the gut
options.D: Overproduction of insulin by the pancreas

correct_answer: B. Blockage of small blood vessels by sickled red cells
why_correct: In sickle cell disease, haemoglobin S polymerises when deoxygenated, distorting red cells into rigid sickle shapes. These cells, with increased adhesion to the endothelium, obstruct small vessels and cause ischaemia and severe pain. Infection, dehydration, cold and hypoxia are classic triggers, as in this case.
why_wrong: A. Antibody-mediated platelet destruction describes immune thrombocytopenia. C. Vitamin K malabsorption causes coagulopathy, not ischaemic pain. D. Insulin excess causes hypoglycaemia. E. Autoimmune neutropenia causes infection risk, not vaso-occlusion.
pearl: Chest pain, fever or new hypoxia in a sickle cell crisis may signal acute chest syndrome, a medical emergency needing urgent senior review.
thinking: Known sickle cell anaemia ↓ Triggers: infection, cold, dehydration ↓ Severe bone and chest pain ↓ Deoxygenated HbS polymerises and red cells sickle ↓ Microvascular occlusion and ischaemia
exam_trap: A, Destruction of platelets in the spleen — the spleen is central to sickle cell disease, which makes this tempting, but the pain arises from sickled cells occluding small vessels.
takeaway: Vaso-occlusive crises result from sickled red cells blocking the microcirculation, causing ischaemic pain.

presentation: Folate deficiency — megaloblastic anaemia without neuropathy
stem:
A 39-year-old man who drinks heavily and eats very few vegetables is found to have a macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils on the film. Neurological examination, including vibration sense and proprioception, is entirely normal.

Which deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia but does not usually cause neurological damage?
correct_answer: D. Folate
why_correct: Both folate and vitamin B12 deficiency impair DNA synthesis and cause megaloblastic anaemia. Only B12 is needed for myelin maintenance, so folate deficiency does not characteristically cause subacute combined degeneration or neuropathy. Poor diet and alcohol excess are common causes of folate deficiency, though B12 should still be checked before giving folic acid.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia, not megaloblastic anaemia. B. Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anaemia. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding gums and perifollicular haemorrhages. E. Vitamin K deficiency causes a coagulopathy.
pearl: Folate stores last only a few months, whereas body B12 stores last several years, so dietary folate deficiency develops much faster.
thinking: Heavy alcohol use and poor diet ↓ Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils ↓ Megaloblastic picture: B12 or folate ↓ Neurology normal ↓ Folate is the deficiency that spares the nervous system
exam_trap: C, Vitamin C — poor diet in heavy drinkers often causes scurvy too, but vitamin C deficiency does not cause megaloblastic anaemia.
takeaway: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia without the neurological damage typical of B12 deficiency.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman with heavy periods attends her GP with tiredness and breathlessness on climbing stairs. Her blood count shows a low haemoglobin with small red cells, and her serum ferritin is below the reference range. Her CRP is normal.

Which condition do these results most strongly indicate?
correct_answer: C. Iron deficiency
why_correct: A microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin indicates depleted iron stores, and a low ferritin is the most specific single test for iron deficiency. Heavy menstrual loss is the likely cause in a premenopausal woman. Treatment is oral iron with a check of response, while considering other causes if the picture does not fit.
why_wrong: A. B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia. B. Haemolysis usually gives a normocytic or macrocytic picture with reticulocytosis and does not lower ferritin. D. Hyperthyroidism does not cause microcytic anaemia with low ferritin. E. Polycythaemia means a raised, not low, haemoglobin.
pearl: A low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, but a normal ferritin does not exclude it when inflammation is present, because ferritin is an acute-phase protein.
thinking: Heavy periods and tiredness ↓ Low haemoglobin with small red cells ↓ Ferritin low, CRP normal ↓ Iron stores depleted ↓ Iron deficiency
exam_trap: A, Vitamin B12 deficiency — it is a common deficiency anaemia in tired young women, but it causes large red cells rather than the microcytosis seen here.
takeaway: Microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency.

stem:
A 55-year-old man with active Crohn's disease has a haemoglobin below the normal range. His CRP is markedly raised and his transferrin saturation is low, but his ferritin is reported as within normal limits. The registrar warns that the ferritin may be giving a false picture of his iron stores.

What is the reason?

options.A: It mainly reflects iron eaten over the previous few days
options.B: It falls during inflammation and so overstates iron deficiency
options.C: It is an acute-phase protein that rises with inflammation
options.D: It measures iron carried in the plasma rather than stored iron
options.E: It is excreted in urine bound to transferrin

correct_answer: C. It is an acute-phase protein that rises with inflammation
why_correct: Ferritin rises as part of the acute-phase response, so active inflammation can push it into the normal range even when iron stores are depleted. In someone with active inflammatory bowel disease, a low transferrin saturation alongside a raised CRP suggests true or functional iron deficiency, and a higher ferritin threshold is used to interpret results.
why_wrong: A. Ferritin reflects stored iron, not recent dietary intake. B. Inflammation increases ferritin rather than lowering it. D. Circulating iron is measured by serum iron and transferrin saturation, not ferritin. E. Ferritin is not lost in the urine bound to transferrin.
pearl: In inflammatory states, transferrin saturation interpreted alongside a concurrent CRP gives a better picture of iron availability than ferritin alone.
thinking: Active inflammatory disease with anaemia ↓ CRP high ↓ Transferrin saturation low ↓ Ferritin falsely reassuring ↓ Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant
exam_trap: B, It falls during inflammation — this reverses the direction; inflammation raises ferritin, which is why it can mask deficiency rather than mimic it.
takeaway: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so a normal level does not exclude iron deficiency during inflammation.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman in a care home has a macrocytic anaemia on blood tests. Staff report that over recent weeks she has become unsteady on her feet and complains of pins and needles in her feet. A colleague suggests starting folic acid straight away.

Which deficiency must be excluded or treated before folic acid is given alone?
correct_answer: A. Vitamin B12
why_correct: Folic acid can partially correct the blood count in vitamin B12 deficiency while the neurological damage, such as subacute combined degeneration of the cord, continues or worsens. Her new unsteadiness and paraesthesia make B12 deficiency particularly likely, so B12 should be checked and, with neurological features, replaced first before folic acid is started alone.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not macrocytic anaemia with neurological signs. C. Calcium deficiency is unrelated to macrocytosis. D. Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anaemia and folic acid does not worsen it. E. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not neuropathy.
pearl: With neurological involvement, hydroxocobalamin is given intramuscularly on alternate days until there is no further improvement, then every two months, with specialist advice.
thinking: Macrocytic anaemia ↓ New unsteadiness and paraesthesia ↓ Suggests B12 deficiency with neurological involvement ↓ Folic acid alone can let neurological damage progress ↓ Exclude or treat B12 first
exam_trap: D, Iron — iron studies are a standard part of any anaemia work-up, but iron deficiency causes microcytosis and is not made more dangerous by giving folic acid.
takeaway: Never give folic acid alone until vitamin B12 deficiency has been excluded or treated, especially with neurological signs.

presentation: Vitamin B12 deficiency in a vegan diet
stem:
A 31-year-old man who has followed a strict plant-based diet without supplements for six years sees his GP because of tingling in both hands, clumsiness and feeling unsteady in the dark. His blood count shows a macrocytic anaemia.

Which deficiency is the most likely explanation?
correct_answer: B. Vitamin B12
why_correct: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal products, so a long-standing vegan diet without fortified foods or supplements can deplete body stores. Deficiency causes a megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia and neurological damage, including peripheral neuropathy and dorsal column loss, which explains the paraesthesia and sensory ataxia worse in the dark.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause neuropathy but typically gives a microcytic, not macrocytic, anaemia. C. Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia and muscle weakness. D. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy. E. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding.
pearl: Dietary B12 deficiency in vegans can be treated with oral cyanocobalamin, but neurological involvement warrants intramuscular hydroxocobalamin first.
thinking: Long-term vegan diet without supplements ↓ B12 comes almost only from animal products ↓ Macrocytic anaemia ↓ Paraesthesia and sensory ataxia ↓ Vitamin B12 deficiency
exam_trap: A, Vitamin B6 — it is also linked to peripheral neuropathy, but B6 deficiency does not produce a macrocytic anaemia.
takeaway: A vegan with macrocytic anaemia and neurological symptoms most likely has vitamin B12 deficiency.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus attends the rheumatology clinic with a week of tiredness and yellowing of her eyes. She is pale and mildly icteric. Her haemoglobin has fallen since her last visit, the reticulocyte count is raised and a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive.

What is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
correct_answer: A. Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
why_correct: A positive direct antiglobulin test shows antibody or complement coating her red cells, so the haemolysis is immune-mediated. SLE is a recognised cause of secondary warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, and the jaundice with reticulocytosis confirms active red-cell destruction with a marrow response.
why_wrong: B. G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-triggered, non-immune haemolysis and the antiglobulin test is negative. C. Aplastic anaemia is marrow failure with a low reticulocyte count and pancytopenia, not haemolysis. D. Iron deficiency does not cause jaundice or a positive antiglobulin test. E. Thalassaemia trait gives lifelong mild microcytosis without new jaundice or red-cell antibodies.
pearl: Warm autoimmune haemolysis is usually IgG-mediated and is linked to SLE, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and drugs; first-line treatment is a corticosteroid such as prednisolone.
thinking: New anaemia with jaundice ↓ Raised reticulocytes point to haemolysis ↓ Positive direct antiglobulin test means immune-mediated ↓ Background SLE is a known trigger ↓ Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
exam_trap: B, G6PD deficiency — it is a classic cause of haemolysis with jaundice, but it is non-immune and would not give a positive antiglobulin test.
takeaway: Haemolysis with a positive direct antiglobulin test means autoimmune haemolytic anaemia until proven otherwise.

presentation: Vitamin B12 deficiency in a vegan diet
stem:
Over the past six months a 29-year-old man has noticed pins and needles in his hands and feet and feels unsteady in the dark. He changed to a strict plant-based diet three years ago and takes no supplements. At his GP surgery, examination shows reduced joint position sense in his toes and Romberg's test is positive. His full blood count shows a raised mean cell volume.

Which nutrient deficiency is most likely?
correct_answer: D. Cobalamin (vitamin B12)
why_correct: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal products, so a long-term strict vegan diet without supplements can deplete it after a few years of falling body stores. Deficiency causes a megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia and damage to the dorsal columns and peripheral nerves, explaining his loss of position sense and positive Romberg's test.
why_wrong: A. Folate is plentiful in plant foods and its deficiency does not cause dorsal column loss. B. Thiamine deficiency causes neuropathy or Wernicke's encephalopathy but not macrocytic anaemia. C. Iron deficiency gives a microcytic picture without sensory ataxia. E. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and weakness, not macrocytosis or proprioceptive loss.
pearl: Liver stores of vitamin B12 last several years, so dietary deficiency in vegans appears long after the change in diet.
thinking: Strict vegan diet without supplements ↓ Macrocytosis on full blood count ↓ Loss of position sense and positive Romberg's test ↓ Dorsal column involvement plus megaloblastic picture ↓ Vitamin B12 deficiency
exam_trap: A, Folic acid — folate deficiency also causes macrocytosis, but plant diets are rich in folate and it does not damage the dorsal columns.
takeaway: Macrocytosis with proprioceptive loss in a strict vegan points to vitamin B12 deficiency.

stem:
At a care home review, a 71-year-old woman with vitiligo is noted to have a smooth red tongue and tingling in her feet. Her full blood count shows a macrocytic anaemia and serum cobalamin is low. She eats a normal mixed diet and has never had bowel surgery.

Which condition most likely explains her deficiency through loss of intrinsic factor?

options.A: Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum

correct_answer: C. Pernicious anaemia
why_correct: Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune gastritis that destroys parietal cells, so intrinsic factor is no longer produced and dietary vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed in the ileum. Her vitiligo suggests an autoimmune tendency, and a normal diet with no surgery makes an absorption problem from intrinsic factor loss the best explanation.
why_wrong: A. Terminal ileal Crohn's disease impairs B12 uptake at the absorption site, but intrinsic factor production is normal. B. Coeliac disease mainly affects the proximal small bowel and more often causes iron or folate deficiency. D. Bacterial overgrowth consumes B12 in the gut lumen rather than reducing intrinsic factor. E. Pancreatic insufficiency can modestly reduce B12 release from binding proteins but does not affect intrinsic factor.
pearl: Intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific for pernicious anaemia; parietal cell antibodies are more sensitive but less specific.
thinking: Macrocytic anaemia with low B12 ↓ Normal diet and no gut surgery ↓ Glossitis and neuropathy from deficiency ↓ Autoimmune background (vitiligo) ↓ Loss of intrinsic factor from parietal cell destruction ↓ Pernicious anaemia
exam_trap: A, Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum — it is a well-known cause of B12 malabsorption, but the problem there is the absorption site, not intrinsic factor production.
takeaway: Pernicious anaemia causes B12 deficiency through autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman has been receiving hydroxocobalamin injections every three months since intrinsic factor antibodies were found two years ago. She now reports weight gain, constipation and feeling cold all the time.

Which associated condition is most likely to account for her new symptoms?
correct_answer: A. Autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis
why_correct: Pernicious anaemia is an organ-specific autoimmune disease and clusters with other autoimmune conditions, most commonly autoimmune thyroid disease. Her weight gain, constipation and cold intolerance are classic hypothyroid symptoms, so thyroid function tests should be checked.
why_wrong: B. Cushing's syndrome can cause weight gain but not cold intolerance and has no autoimmune link with pernicious anaemia. C. Haemochromatosis is an inherited iron overload disorder, not autoimmune. D. Polycystic ovary syndrome is not linked with pernicious anaemia and does not cause cold intolerance. E. Hyperparathyroidism causes constipation but not cold intolerance and is not an autoimmune association.
pearl: Pernicious anaemia is also associated with type 1 diabetes, vitiligo and Addison's disease, and carries an increased risk of gastric cancer.
thinking: Known pernicious anaemia ↓ Autoimmune disease clusters together ↓ New weight gain, constipation and cold intolerance ↓ Features of hypothyroidism ↓ Autoimmune thyroiditis
exam_trap: E, Primary hyperparathyroidism — constipation and tiredness may tempt, but it does not cause cold intolerance and is not part of the autoimmune cluster.
takeaway: Patients with pernicious anaemia should be watched for other autoimmune disease, especially thyroid disease.

stem:
Ten days after an upper gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal ulcer, a 61-year-old man returns to the medical day unit for repeat bloods. He has had no further melaena. His haemoglobin is still below normal but slightly higher than at discharge, and the reticulocyte count is now well above the reference range. Bilirubin is normal.

What does the raised reticulocyte count best reflect?

options.A: Infiltration of the marrow by malignant cells
options.B: Lack of erythropoietin from kidney failure
options.C: Megaloblastic change from vitamin B12 deficiency
options.D: Appropriately increased marrow red-cell output in response to blood loss

correct_answer: D. Appropriately increased marrow red-cell output in response to blood loss
why_correct: Reticulocytes are newly released red cells, and a high count means the marrow is working hard to replace lost cells. After an acute haemorrhage this rise appears within days and peaks around a week or so later, matching his slowly recovering haemoglobin. The normal bilirubin suggests the cells were lost by bleeding rather than destroyed by haemolysis.
why_wrong: A. Marrow infiltration reduces red-cell production and gives a low reticulocyte count. B. Erythropoietin deficiency in kidney disease causes a hypoproliferative anaemia with low reticulocytes. C. B12 deficiency causes ineffective erythropoiesis with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count. E. Inflammation suppresses erythropoiesis, so reticulocytes would be low.
pearl: A raised reticulocyte count points to bleeding or haemolysis; a low count in anaemia points to reduced production (deficiency, marrow failure or kidney disease).
thinking: Anaemia after an acute bleed ↓ Reticulocytes now well above normal ↓ High count means the marrow is producing more ↓ Normal bilirubin argues against haemolysis ↓ Appropriate marrow response to blood loss
exam_trap: C, Megaloblastic change from vitamin B12 deficiency — any anaemia may tempt a nutritional answer, but B12 deficiency gives a low reticulocyte count.
takeaway: A high reticulocyte count in anaemia shows an active marrow responding to red-cell loss or destruction.

presentation: Blood film in iron deficiency anaemia
stem:
A 38-year-old woman who donates blood regularly is deferred because of a low haemoglobin on screening. She feels more tired than usual and gets breathless climbing stairs. Her GP confirms an anaemia with a low mean cell volume and low ferritin.

Which appearance is most likely on her blood film?

options.D: Small, pale (microcytic, hypochromic) red cells with pencil cells

correct_answer: D. Small, pale (microcytic, hypochromic) red cells with pencil cells
why_correct: Repeated blood donation can deplete iron stores, and low ferritin confirms iron deficiency. Without enough iron, haemoglobin synthesis falls, producing small red cells with reduced central colour. Elongated pencil cells are also typical of iron deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Schistocytes suggest mechanical or microangiopathic haemolysis. B. Macrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils indicate B12 or folate deficiency. C. Spherocytes are seen in hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis. E. Sickle cells occur in sickle cell disease, not acquired iron deficiency.
