pearl: In iron deficiency the red cell distribution width is usually raised, which helps distinguish it from thalassaemia trait where cells are uniformly small.
thinking: Regular blood donor with fatigue ↓ Low MCV and low ferritin ↓ Iron deficiency anaemia ↓ Impaired haemoglobin synthesis ↓ Microcytic, hypochromic cells with pencil cells on the film
exam_trap: C, Spherocytes — they also look small and dense, but they lack central pallor and point to haemolysis, not iron deficiency.
takeaway: Iron deficiency anaemia gives a microcytic, hypochromic blood film.

stem:
A 9-month-old boy of Cypriot heritage is seen in the paediatric clinic with poor feeding, pallor and an enlarging abdomen. His spleen and liver are palpable. Haemoglobin is very low with marked microcytosis, and his parents are both known carriers of a haemoglobin disorder. He is likely to need red-cell transfusions every few weeks for life.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.D: Iron deficiency from early cow's milk

correct_answer: C. Beta-thalassaemia major
why_correct: Beta-thalassaemia major results from inheriting two defective beta-globin genes, so symptoms appear as fetal haemoglobin falls in the second half of the first year. Severe ineffective erythropoiesis causes profound microcytic anaemia and hepatosplenomegaly, and lifelong regular transfusion is needed. Two carrier parents and Mediterranean ancestry fit.
why_wrong: A. Alpha-thalassaemia trait causes mild microcytosis without transfusion need. B. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis with spherocytes and is usually not severe enough to need regular lifelong transfusion. D. Dietary iron deficiency improves with iron and does not cause hepatosplenomegaly or need long-term transfusion. E. G6PD deficiency causes episodic haemolysis with triggers, not continuous transfusion dependence.
pearl: Regular transfusion in thalassaemia major leads to iron overload, so iron chelation with desferrioxamine or deferasirox is an essential part of care.
thinking: Infant with severe anaemia after fetal haemoglobin falls ↓ Marked microcytosis ↓ Hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis ↓ Two carrier parents, Mediterranean heritage ↓ Lifelong transfusion need ↓ Beta-thalassaemia major
exam_trap: B, Hereditary spherocytosis — it is inherited and can cause anaemia and splenomegaly, but it rarely requires lifelong regular transfusion and is not markedly microcytic.
takeaway: Severe inherited microcytic anaemia needing lifelong transfusion from infancy is classic beta-thalassaemia major.

presentation: Iron studies in anaemia of chronic disease
stem:
A 57-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis and persistently raised inflammatory markers is seen in clinic with a mild normocytic anaemia. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms. The team suspect the anaemia is driven by his inflammatory disease rather than iron loss.

Which set of iron studies would best support this?

options.A: Low ferritin and raised transferrin saturation
options.B: Low ferritin, low serum iron and raised total iron-binding capacity
options.C: Raised ferritin with very high transferrin saturation
options.D: Normal iron studies with a low vitamin B12
options.E: Low serum iron and low total iron-binding capacity with normal or raised ferritin

correct_answer: E. Low serum iron and low total iron-binding capacity with normal or raised ferritin
why_correct: Inflammation stimulates hepcidin, which traps iron in macrophages and blocks gut absorption, so circulating iron falls while stores remain normal or high. Ferritin is also an acute phase protein, so it is normal or raised, and transferrin (total iron-binding capacity) is reduced. This pattern fits anaemia of chronic disease.
why_wrong: A. Low ferritin means depleted stores and would not come with a raised transferrin saturation. B. This is the typical pattern of true iron deficiency. C. High ferritin with very high saturation suggests iron overload such as haemochromatosis. D. A low B12 would point to a separate cause and would usually give macrocytosis.
pearl: In inflammation, a ferritin in the low-normal range does not exclude iron deficiency, because ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant.
thinking: Chronic inflammatory disease with mild anaemia ↓ Hepcidin rises ↓ Iron trapped in stores, serum iron falls ↓ Ferritin normal or high, TIBC low ↓ Anaemia of chronic disease pattern
exam_trap: B, Low ferritin, low serum iron and raised TIBC — low serum iron is shared, but the low ferritin and high TIBC point to true iron deficiency.
takeaway: Anaemia of chronic disease shows low serum iron with preserved or raised ferritin and low TIBC.

presentation: Neurological features of vitamin B12 deficiency
stem:
A 44-year-old man who had an ileal resection for Crohn's disease several years ago stopped attending for his injections. He now attends the GP with tiredness and a sore, smooth tongue, and his blood count shows macrocytosis with a low serum cobalamin.

Which neurological symptom is he most at risk of developing as a result of this deficiency?

options.A: Symmetrical tingling and numbness in the feet
options.B: Painless loss of vision in one eye
options.D: Sudden weakness of one side of the face

correct_answer: A. Symmetrical tingling and numbness in the feet
why_correct: Removal of the terminal ileum prevents B12 absorption, so lifelong replacement is needed. Deficiency damages peripheral nerves and the dorsal columns, typically starting with symmetrical paraesthesia and numbness in the feet, later with loss of vibration and position sense.
why_wrong: B. Sudden monocular visual loss suggests a vascular or demyelinating cause; B12-related optic neuropathy is rare and usually bilateral. C. Resting tremor is a parkinsonian sign. D. Unilateral facial weakness suggests Bell's palsy or stroke. E. Focal seizures point to a structural brain lesion rather than B12 deficiency.
pearl: Patients with B12 deficiency and neurological involvement need hydroxocobalamin injections on alternate days until no further improvement, as advised by the BNF.
thinking: Ileal resection with missed B12 replacement ↓ Glossitis and macrocytosis ↓ Low serum cobalamin ↓ B12 damages peripheral nerves and dorsal columns ↓ Symmetrical distal paraesthesia
exam_trap: B, Painless loss of vision in one eye — optic neuropathy can rarely occur, but it is usually bilateral and much less common than distal paraesthesia.
takeaway: The commonest neurological feature of vitamin B12 deficiency is symmetrical distal paraesthesia.

stem:
A 7-year-old girl with hereditary spherocytosis is brought to the emergency department by her father. She had a mild fever and runny nose a week ago, and today she is very pale, lethargic and breathless on walking. Her haemoglobin has fallen far below her usual level and, unusually for her, the reticulocyte count is almost undetectable.

Which infection is the most likely trigger?
correct_answer: D. Parvovirus B19
why_correct: Parvovirus B19 infects and destroys red-cell precursors, briefly stopping erythropoiesis. In a child whose red cells already have a shortened lifespan from chronic haemolysis, this causes a rapid, severe fall in haemoglobin with very few reticulocytes, which is a transient aplastic crisis. Transfusion is often needed until the marrow recovers.
why_wrong: A. Epstein-Barr virus can trigger haemolysis or splenic problems but does not typically switch off red-cell production. B. Influenza does not selectively infect erythroid precursors. C. Hepatitis A causes an acute hepatitis and does not selectively halt red-cell production in this way. E. Mycoplasma causes cold-antibody haemolysis, which would raise the reticulocyte count.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis can occur in any chronic haemolytic anaemia, including sickle cell disease and hereditary spherocytosis; household contacts with the same condition should be monitored.
thinking: Chronic haemolytic anaemia ↓ Recent viral prodrome ↓ Sudden severe drop in haemoglobin ↓ Reticulocytes almost absent, so production has stopped ↓ Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
exam_trap: E, Mycoplasma pneumoniae — it does cause haemolysis after a respiratory illness, but haemolysis drives reticulocytes up, not down.
takeaway: A sudden severe anaemia with very low reticulocytes in chronic haemolysis suggests a parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong C claimed hepatitis A is a recognised (rare) cause of aplastic anaemia; hepatitis-associated aplasia is usually non-A non-B, so reworded to 'does not selectively halt red-cell production'.

stem:
On the acute medical unit, a 63-year-old man is found to have large red cells and a low haemoglobin. Haematinic levels have been sent but will not be reported until tomorrow, and the registrar asks you to examine him carefully.

Which bedside finding would make cobalamin, rather than folic acid, the more likely missing vitamin?

options.D: Loss of vibration sense and joint position sense in the legs

correct_answer: D. Loss of vibration sense and joint position sense in the legs
why_correct: Both deficiencies cause a megaloblastic anaemia with similar blood and general findings. Only vitamin B12 deficiency typically causes neurological damage, such as subacute combined degeneration of the cord with loss of vibration and position sense, so this sign favours B12.
why_wrong: A. Glossitis occurs with both B12 and folate deficiency. B. Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from ineffective erythropoiesis occurs in both. C. Exertional breathlessness reflects anaemia of any cause. E. Pallor is a non-specific sign of anaemia.
pearl: If both are low, replace vitamin B12 before or alongside folic acid, as folic acid alone may worsen B12-related neurological damage.
thinking: Macrocytic anaemia ↓ B12 and folate both possible ↓ Blood and general findings overlap ↓ Neurological signs are specific to B12 ↓ Dorsal column loss favours B12 deficiency
exam_trap: A, A smooth, sore tongue — glossitis is often taught with B12 deficiency, but folate deficiency causes it equally.
takeaway: Neurological signs, especially dorsal column loss, point to vitamin B12 rather than folate deficiency.

presentation: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult
stem:
An 80-year-old woman's routine bloods before cataract surgery show a microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin. She eats well, has been postmenopausal for decades and reports no bleeding, indigestion or change in bowel habit.

Which cause is most important to look for?

options.E: Occult bleeding from a gastrointestinal lesion

correct_answer: E. Occult bleeding from a gastrointestinal lesion
why_correct: Iron deficiency in a postmenopausal woman with a good diet has no ordinary explanation, so chronic hidden blood loss from the gut, including colorectal or gastric cancer, must be considered. Absence of symptoms does not exclude a tumour, and NICE suspected cancer guidance supports urgent investigation of unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Thalassaemia trait gives lifelong microcytosis with normal ferritin. B. Kidney-related anaemia is usually normocytic with normal ferritin. C. B12 malabsorption causes macrocytic, not microcytic, anaemia. D. Sideroblastic anaemia is rare and usually has normal or high ferritin.
pearl: Coeliac serology should also be checked in unexplained iron deficiency, as malabsorption is another important cause.
thinking: Microcytic anaemia with low ferritin ↓ Older, postmenopausal, good diet ↓ No obvious source of loss ↓ Occult gastrointestinal bleeding including cancer ↓ Needs urgent investigation
exam_trap: A, Alpha-thalassaemia trait — it also gives microcytosis, but the low ferritin confirms true iron deficiency.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 50-year-old man who lives alone and drinks several cans of strong cider every day is admitted with a fall. His diet consists mainly of crisps and toast. He has no numbness, tingling or unsteadiness, and neurological examination is normal. His blood count shows a macrocytic anaemia.

Which deficiency is most likely contributing?
correct_answer: C. Folate
why_correct: Heavy drinking with a poor diet is a classic cause of folate deficiency, because intake is low and alcohol interferes with folate absorption and metabolism. Folate deficiency causes a megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia, and the absence of neurological features fits better than B12 deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum and skin bleeding, not macrocytosis. B. Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anaemia. D. Vitamin K deficiency causes a bleeding tendency with a prolonged INR, not anaemia with large cells. E. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and dry eyes.
pearl: Alcohol itself can raise the mean cell volume even without folate deficiency, so check folate, B12, liver function and thyroid function in macrocytosis.
thinking: Heavy alcohol use and poor diet ↓ Macrocytic anaemia ↓ No neurological features ↓ Low intake and impaired metabolism of folate ↓ Folate deficiency
exam_trap: B, Iron — poor diet suggests iron deficiency, but that would cause small red cells, not macrocytosis.
takeaway: Alcohol excess with poor nutrition is a common cause of folate-deficient macrocytic anaemia.
